title: Network Topology and Tenant Isolation Guidelines
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary

Purpose: Define standardized network topology patterns and tenant isolation controls used across Redwood Inference deployments (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private). This doc codifies: failure-domain mapping, recommended intra-cluster networking, cross-region routing policies, and how those choices map to API, coding, observability, and performance standards.

Audience: infra architects, platform engineers, runtime team, security, SREs, and product owners planning Dedicated/Private deployments.

Goals
- Provide a single, actionable reference for designing tenant isolation without impacting latency SLOs.
- Reduce cognitive overhead when onboarding new customers or spinning up Dedicated pools.
- Make trade-offs between cost, isolation, and performance explicit and repeatable.

Non-goals
- This is not a cloud-provider specific how-to for every edge case. Provider-specific runbooks live in eng-private-deployments.

Principles (short)
1) Least-privilege networking: default-deny egress and ingress at the tenant boundary.
2) Failure-domain separation: map compute, storage, and network failure domains to explicit SLOs.
3) Observable boundaries: every isolation boundary must emit metrics and tracing spans.
4) Consistent API behavior: isolation must be transparent to client API semantics; logical fallbacks must be explicit.

High-level topology patterns
- Shared-hosted (low isolation, lowest cost): multi-tenant service mesh, logical namespace isolation, token-level request routing.
- Tenant-dedicated (medium isolation): per-tenant Kubernetes namespace + network policies + dedicated model-serving pods on shared GPU nodes with cgroup isolation.
- Node-dedicated / VPC-isolated (high isolation): dedicated GPU pools in a customer VPC or on-prem rack, private control plane, separate routing and KMS keys.

Failure domain mapping (recommended)
| Domain | Example components | Owner | Typical SLO mapping |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Instance | VM/Node, NIC, local GPU | infra | p99 availability per node: 99.9% |
| Availability zone | AZ-level power/network | cloud / infra | Regional redis failover: 99.95% |
| Cluster | K8s controlplane, CNI, API server | platform | Control-plane operations: p95 restart < 30s |
| Tenant namespace | Network policy, pods | runtime | API p95 latency unaffected; isolation errors < 0.1% |

Network segmentation model (recommended defaults)
- Management plane: separate VLAN/VPC for control plane (console, billing, admin APIs). No customer workload egress permitted without explicit ACLs.
- Data plane: customer inference traffic flows through edge layer -> model-router -> serving pool. Each tenant maps to one of three tiers: shared, dedicated, or isolated.
- Shared-tier uses service-mesh sidecars with mTLS and per-token auth. Dedicated-tier uses namespace-level network policies with egress restrictions; optionally, IP-based ACLs for high compliance tenants.

Tenant isolation patterns and trade-offs
1) Logical namespace isolation (default for Hosted API)
   - Pros: low cost, fast scaling, simple rollouts.
   - Cons: noisy neighbor risk; requires strong runtime KV/prefix caching policies and QoS.

2) Node pinning with soft cgroups (Dedicated)
   - Pros: improved tail-latency predictability, easier capacity accounting.
   - Cons: more engineering for bin-packing and autoscaling.

3) Physical hardware isolation (Private/VPC)
   - Pros: maximum regulatory compliance and data residency guarantees.
   - Cons: highest cost, slower elasticity.

API standards alignment
- Service contracts must not expose topology changes to the API consumer. If a request routes to a fallback model or different tier due to capacity, the response must include a standard header/metadata field: "x-redwood-serving-tier" with values [shared,dedicated,isolation-fallback].
- Errors caused by isolation (e.g., tenant egress blocked) should return typed errors per the typed-error-model doc (see related_pages) with remediation hints.

Coding and infra conventions (practical)
- All services that touch tenant-anchored state must be annotated with a standard tenant label: "redwood.tenant_id".
- Network ACLs and policies must be managed as code (in terraform/helm charts) and stored in the infra repo with PR review and automated policy tests.
- Use the platform’s QoS classes: "latency-critical", "throughput", "best-effort". Map model-serving gRPC workers to "latency-critical".

Observability and SLO mapping
- Per-tenant metrics required: request_rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, error_rate (by error class), kv_cache_hit_rate, model_fallback_rate.
- Default SLOs (apply unless product contract overrides):
  - API availability: 99.95% monthly for hosted; 99.9% for dedicated pools (contract-level).
  - Latency (short generation path): p95 < 150ms, p99 < 500ms for <512 tokens on latency-critical tier.
  - Error budget: max 0.1% elevated errors for latency-critical services per month.
- Tracing: every cross-boundary request must add a span with tags: tenant_id, serving_tier, model_id, route_id.
- Alerting: create tenant-scoped alerts when p99 latency exceeds 2x SLO or when fallback_rate > 1% for 5 min.

Performance budgets and capacity planning
- Budgeting inputs: expected qps per tenant, average tokens per request, burst profile (95/99 percentile concurrency).
- Example capacity rule-of-thumb: 1x A100-equivalent GPU (int8) serves ~250 concurrent generation requests (avg seq len 64) with target p95 < 200ms. Tune via benchmarking harness.

Deployment and rollout checklist (minimum for new Dedicated pool)
1) Create tenant namespace with labels and apply default-deny network policy.
2) Provision GPU nodes and set taints/tolerations for model-serving pods.
3) Apply QoS class priorities to serving pods and configure podDisruptionBudgets.
4) Enable per-tenant metric collection and tracing; verify dashboards.
5) Run synthetic traffic test against a canary model and measure p95/p99.
6) Run security scan and confirm KMS integration and audit logging.

Quick example: namespace network policy (Kubernetes, Cilium-friendly)

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-incoming
  namespace: tenant-1234
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress: []
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          redwood: model-router
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080

Operational commands and checks
- Verify namespace isolation: kubectl get networkpolicy -n tenant-1234
- Simulate tenant egress block (debug): curl --interface <pod-ip> https://public-eval.example.com || log and alert
- Capacity smoke test (local): loadgen --target http://model-router/serve --qps 200 --concurrency 50 --duration 60s

Audit, compliance and evidence collection
- Required artifacts for Dedicated/Private delivery: network-policy manifests, KMS key IDs, VPC peering configs, audit logs for control-plane operations (90 days), and signed runbook acceptance by customer security.
- Logging retention: default 90d for hosted, configurable for Dedicated under contract.

Escalation and ownership
- First responder: runtime-oncall (rotate via eng-sre schedule).
- Platform network owner: infra-netteam@redwood.com.
- Security escalation: security-ops@redwood.com.

Appendix: mapping to other standards and ADRs
- This guideline expects services to follow the API compatibility and typed-error recommendations and to emit telemetry per observability SLI standards (see related pages).
- If a deployment requires deviation (e.g., air-gapped cryptography), capture an ADR with rationale and risk mitigations.

- 2025-04-22: added per-tenant alert thresholds and example policies (review by L. Zhang)
